skill.name: onvifscan
skill.description: Guides authorized ONVIF device security testing, including authentication checks and controlled credential auditing with the onvifscan CLI.
skill.summary: Run authorized ONVIF authentication checks and credential audits with the onvifscan CLI.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: The static backtick and hardcoded-address alerts are documentation false positives. Semantic review found high-risk dual-use behavior: ONVIF credential brute forcing, potentially destructive endpoint testing, and no required authorization gate.

remediation.suggestion: Require explicit authorization, scope, and consent before any brute-force scan. Limit examples to owned lab devices and document legal constraints.
Default away from the all-endpoint option, require explicit confirmation, and list expected side effects before execution.
Tell agents to show commands for approval before execution and to avoid scans until the user confirms authorization.

semantic_findings.title: Credential Brute Forcing Capability
semantic_findings.description: The skill directs the agent to run credential brute-force scans against ONVIF endpoints and supports custom wordlists. This can enable unauthorized access if used outside owned devices.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The documented brute mode and custom wordlist example clearly support credential guessing against ONVIF devices.

semantic_findings.title: Potentially Destructive Endpoint Testing
semantic_findings.description: The skill offers an option to test all endpoints, including potentially destructive ones. Running this against production cameras could change device state or disrupt service.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The file explicitly labels the all-endpoint option as potentially destructive and tells users to use it with caution.

semantic_findings.title: Missing Authorization Gate for Network Scans
semantic_findings.description: The workflow asks for target details and scan type but does not require proof of ownership or authorization before scanning. This increases misuse risk for third-party devices.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The instructions proceed from a user scan request to target collection and command execution without an explicit authorization check.

content.value_statement: IP cameras can expose ONVIF services with weak authentication. This skill guides authorized checks with onvifscan and explains safer scan choices.
actual_capabilities: Explains auth and brute scan modes for ONVIF devices.
Collects target URL, scan type, and optional wordlist choices.
Shows onvifscan command formats for common assessments.
Describes verbose, output format, and endpoint coverage options.
Highlights caution for destructive endpoint checks and rate limits.
limitations: Requires the onvifscan CLI and its wordlists to be installed.
Does not verify legal authorization for a target.
Does not provide device-specific remediation steps after findings.
Can cause disruption if unsafe options are used on production devices.

use_cases.title: Lab Camera Assessment
use_cases.description: A security student checks owned test cameras for open ONVIF endpoints.

use_cases.title: Fleet Credential Audit
use_cases.description: An internal security team reviews weak default credentials across approved camera assets.

use_cases.title: Predeployment Review
use_cases.description: An integrator validates camera authentication before installation at a customer site.

prompt_templates.title: Run an Auth Check
prompt_templates.prompt: Use this skill to plan an authorized ONVIF auth check for one camera. Ask before running any command.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Scan Modes
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain when to use auth mode or brute mode for an owned ONVIF camera. Include risks and safer defaults.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare Custom Wordlists
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan a credential audit for approved ONVIF devices using custom usernames and passwords. Include scope, limits, and confirmation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Review Production Safety
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a cautious scan plan for a production ONVIF camera fleet. Include authorization checks, rate limits, and rollback considerations.

output_examples.input: Scan planning request for one owned camera.
output_examples.output: The response identifies auth mode as the first step, asks for confirmation, and notes that brute mode needs explicit approval.
The response asks for approved scope, wordlist locations, attempt limits, and monitoring contacts before any scan.
The response warns about destructive endpoint tests and recommends a maintenance window and backup plan.

best_practices: Confirm ownership, scope, and written authorization before scanning any device.
Start with auth mode before any credential audit.
Use small, approved wordlists and monitor device health during testing.
anti_patterns: Do not scan public or third-party cameras without written authorization.
Do not use all-endpoint testing on production devices without a maintenance window.
Do not treat brute-force results as proof of full device security.

faq.question: What does this skill help with?
faq.answer: It guides authorized ONVIF authentication checks and credential audits using onvifscan.

faq.question: Is this safe for production cameras?
faq.answer: Use caution. Auth checks are safer, but all-endpoint and brute-force tests can disrupt devices.

faq.question: Does it install onvifscan?
faq.answer: No. The CLI and wordlists must already be available in the environment.

faq.question: Can it test devices I do not own?
faq.answer: No. Use it only on devices where you have explicit authorization.

faq.question: Does it fix discovered weaknesses?
faq.answer: No. It helps identify authentication exposure and weak credentials, then you must apply vendor remediation.

faq.question: Which tools can use it?
faq.answer: It is declared for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
